mcqs.question: What actually happens when you execute s += x on an immutable string?
options: The characters of x are appended into the existing memory block that s occupies
A new block is allocated, s's contents and x's contents are both copied into it, and s is repointed to it
Nothing is copied — s and x are linked via a pointer chain
x is copied but s's original characters are reused in place
mcqs.explanation: Immutability means the original string object can never change, so the runtime must build an entirely new object holding both s and x's characters and reassign the variable to it. Nothing about the original memory block is reused or modified.

mcqs.question: A loop runs s += chunk n times, where s grows by a roughly constant amount each time. What's the total complexity?
options: O(n), since each iteration only adds a constant-size chunk
O(n log n), from the repeated reallocation
O(log n), because the buffer eventually stabilizes
O(n²), because the k-th append copies roughly k units of data, and those costs sum to a triangular number
mcqs.explanation: Each append copies everything accumulated so far, so cost grows with the iteration number; summing 1+2+...+n gives n(n+1)/2, which is Θ(n²). The chunk size being constant doesn't save you — it's the size of the accumulated string being copied that matters, not the size of the new piece.

mcqs.question: Why does the quadratic cost of a string-building loop often go unnoticed in code review?
options: Each individual += line looks like a constant-time operation, hiding the fact that its cost grows with every prior iteration
Most languages raise a compile warning only above a size threshold that reviewers ignore
String concatenation is always O(1) unless the loop has a nested loop inside it
The bug only manifests when strings contain non-ASCII characters
mcqs.explanation: There's no visible nested loop — just one line executed n times — so nothing in the syntax signals that the line's cost depends on how much has already been built. There's no such compiler warning, and encoding has nothing to do with it.

mcqs.question: In build_fast (append each word to a list, then "".join(parts)), what is the overall complexity for n words?
options: O(n²), same as the naive version, just with different syntax
O(n log n), from sorting the parts before joining
O(n), because appends are amortized O(1) and the join is a single linear pass
O(1), because join defers all work until the string is printed
mcqs.explanation: Appending to a mutable list is amortized O(1) per call, and join makes exactly one pass copying each character once — both stages are linear, so the total is O(n). There's no sorting involved and join does real work immediately, not lazily.

mcqs.question: A C++ loop does result += word for n words using std::string. Is this quadratic like the Python/Java naive version?
options: Yes, identically — immutability is a universal property of strings across languages
No, only if the compiler happens to inline the loop
Yes, but only for strings longer than a few hundred characters
No — std::string is mutable with its own amortized-growth buffer, so += there behaves like a dynamic array append, not a reallocate-everything operation
mcqs.explanation: C++'s std::string owns a growable buffer and appends into spare capacity the same way a vector does, so it isn't quadratic here. The quadratic bug is specifically a consequence of immutability, which std::string doesn't have — it's not a universal string property.
